lead: Automotive embedded systems control the car with electronic control units (ECUs), sensors and in-vehicle buses. They must meet hard deadlines, stay safe when a part fails, and cost little. Smart sensors do filtering and calibration locally. Driver-assistance systems build a pipeline: sensors, conditioning, fusion, perception, decision and actuator. Adaptive cruise control uses radar to keep a time gap from the car ahead. In dense traffic, cut-ins and mixed vehicle sizes make latency and false alarms visible.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.5 for partitioning, Unit 3 for sensors and ADCs, and Unit 4 for CAN and LIN buses.

blocks.text: An electronic control unit (ECU) is a small computer with a microcontroller, power supply, input protection and output drivers. It runs fixed-period control loops: read sensors, compute, drive actuators, repeat. Engine, brakes, steering and body functions use separate ECUs.

CAN (Controller Area Network) is a multi-master broadcast bus. Nodes send frames with identifiers; lower identifiers win arbitration. CAN is used for fast control signals. LIN (Local Interconnect Network) is a cheaper single-wire bus for switches, mirrors and seats; it is not for safety-critical braking. Software must handle bus timeouts, checksums and missing frames. A late brake command is a fault, not a slow response.

In a car, wiring length and weight matter. A shared bus replaces many point-to-point wires. Each ECU needs a communication stack and a watchdog. The control loop period is chosen from the physical process: a current controller may run faster than a temperature controller. The designer checks worst-case execution time plus bus delay against the deadline.

A smart sensor contains the sensing element, signal conditioning, an analog-to-digital converter (ADC), a small processor and a bus interface. Signal conditioning amplifies a weak signal, removes noise with a filter, and protects against voltage spikes. The processor converts raw counts to engineering units, for example metres or degrees Celsius.

Calibration removes offset and gain error. A simple model is y = a·x + b. Here x is the raw reading, y is the corrected value, a is the gain and b is the offset. The values of a and b are found during factory test and stored in non-volatile memory. At run time the sensor applies them before sending data. A smart sensor can also flag saturation, open circuit or out-of-range readings. This reduces the load on the ECU and shortens the wire from the sensing point.
Smart sensors send data over I2C, SPI or CAN. The ECU then trusts the sensor's status bits and plausibility checks.

Driver assistance uses several sensors because no single sensor is enough. Radar measures range and relative speed and works in rain and darkness. Camera reads lane marks, signs and objects but needs light. Lidar builds a 3D point cloud with direct distance. Ultrasonic covers short parking distances. Conditioning filters each raw signal and rejects invalid pulses. Fusion combines the estimates with weights or probabilistic filters. Perception turns fused data into objects, lanes and free space. Decision plans speed and path. Actuator commands throttle, brake or steering.

blocks.text: Time gap T<sub>gap</sub> is how long the host takes to reach the present position of the car ahead. Time to collision TTC is how long until the gap closes. Latency matters: sensor exposure, ADC conversion, CAN transfer, fusion, decision and actuator delay all add to reaction time. The gap must include them.

sections.h3: Functional safety and a case study

blocks.text: Functional safety asks what happens when a sensor, ECU or bus fails. Common measures are a watchdog timer, memory and program-flow checks, end-to-end protection on CAN frames, redundant sensors and a safe fallback state. A plausible but wrong reading is dangerous; software compares radar range with camera size and vehicle speed. Standards such as ISO 26262 define safety levels, but the exam idea is simple: detect faults, fail safely, and keep the driver informed.

Case study: adaptive cruise control. Radar tracks a car 40 m ahead. Host speed is 25 m/s and target speed is 20 m/s. The host computes time gap 1.6 s, closing speed 5 m/s, time to collision 8 s. A 2 s desired gap at 25 m/s is 50 m. Since 40 m is less than 50 m, the controller reduces throttle or applies a mild brake. It does not wait for TTC to reach zero. The same loop runs repeatedly; each cycle rechecks the gap.

figure.caption: Radar data is conditioned, fused with speed estimates, perceived as a lead car, compared with a 50 m desired gap, and sent to throttle or brake. Notice the 40 m measured gap is below the 50 m target.

examples.question: An adaptive cruise control radar measures a car 40 m ahead. The host car travels at 25 m/s and the car ahead at 20 m/s. Find (a) the time gap, (b) the relative speed, (c) the time to collision, and (d) the distance for a desired 2 s gap. State the control action if the desired gap is larger than the measured gap.
steps: Identify the data: measured distance d = 40 m, host speed v<sub>host</sub> = 25 m/s, target speed v<sub>target</sub> = 20 m/s, desired time gap T<sub>desired</sub> = 2 s.
Time gap T<sub>gap</sub> = d ÷ v<sub>host</sub> = 40 m ÷ 25 m/s = 1.6 s.
Relative speed = v<sub>host</sub> − v<sub>target</sub> = 25 m/s − 20 m/s = 5 m/s.
Time to collision TTC = d ÷ relative speed = 40 m ÷ 5 m/s = 8 s.
Desired gap D = v<sub>host</sub> × T<sub>desired</sub> = 25 m/s × 2 s = 50 m.
Compare: measured gap 40 m is less than desired gap 50 m, so the controller should reduce throttle or apply a mild brake.
examples.answer: Time gap = 1.6 s, relative speed = 5 m/s, time to collision = 8 s, desired 2 s gap = 50 m; since 40 m < 50 m, the controller should reduce throttle or brake.
examples.check:
host = 25.0
target = 20.0
d = 40.0
T_desired = 2.0
time_gap = d / host
relative = host - target
ttc = d / relative
desired = host * T_desired
print(time_gap)
print(relative)
print(ttc)
print(desired)

traps: Time gap uses host speed only; time to collision uses relative speed. Mixing the two gives a wrong answer.
The desired gap uses host speed and desired time, not the measured gap and not relative speed.
Ignoring sensor, CAN and actuator latency makes a gap look safe when the reaction is late.
Radar gives range and relative speed; camera gives size, class and lane. Fusion does not remove the need for calibration.
LIN is a low-cost body bus, not a replacement for CAN in braking or steering.

quiz.q: What is an ECU? Name two parts inside it.
quiz.a: An electronic control unit is a small computer for one vehicle function. It contains a microcontroller, power supply, input protection, output drivers, memory and software.

quiz.q: Why does a car use CAN instead of separate wires for every switch and sensor?
quiz.a: A shared CAN bus reduces wiring weight, cost and connectors. It broadcasts frames, supports priority arbitration and lets many ECUs share signals. Software must still check timeouts and checksums.

quiz.q: Radar sees a car 30 m ahead. Host speed is 20 m/s and target speed is 15 m/s. Find the time gap and the time to collision.
quiz.a: Time gap = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 s. Relative speed = 20 − 15 = 5 m/s. Time to collision = 30 ÷ 5 = 6 s.

quiz.q: Why fuse radar and camera for automatic emergency braking?
quiz.a: Radar gives robust range and relative speed in rain and darkness. Camera gives object class, lane position and shape. Fusion reduces false positives and missed detections, but the design must handle calibration, latency and disagreement between sensors.

quiz.q: In the smart-sensor model y = a·x + b, what do x, y, a and b mean?
quiz.a: x is the raw reading, y is the corrected value, a is the gain and b is the offset. The sensor finds a and b during calibration and stores them in non-volatile memory.

quiz.q: A car wants a 2.5 s time gap at 24 m/s. What distance should it keep?
quiz.a: Desired distance = v<sub>host</sub> × T<sub>desired</sub> = 24 m/s × 2.5 s = 60 m.

quiz.q: Give two reasons to include worst-case latency in adaptive cruise control.
quiz.a: Sensor exposure, ADC conversion, CAN transfer, fusion, decision and actuator delay all consume time before braking acts. A gap that is safe on paper can become unsafe if latency is omitted. The controller must keep extra distance or react earlier to meet the real deadline.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars are moving to zonal electrical architectures with automotive Ethernet and central compute. ADAS software uses middleware and over-the-air updates. Safety-of-the-intended-function work addresses perception limits that are not hardware faults. Search terms: AUTOSAR, ISO 26262, ISO 21448, sensor fusion, adaptive cruise control.
